title: Probability and Risk
summary: Interpreting probability in contexts such as gambling, insurance, medical tests and weather; two-way tables and tree diagrams; expected value; and evaluating risk and fairness.

items: **Weather**: '40% chance of rain' means rain fell on about 40 out of 100 similar days in the past.
**Lotteries**: the chance of winning the jackpot is tiny, while the expected return on each ticket is less than its price.
**Insurance**: premiums are set using the probability of claims in a large group.
**Health**: risk factors (smoking, diet) change the probability of disease.

notes.latex: \text{expected value per game} = (\text{probability of winning} \times \text{prize}) - \text{cost to play}

notes.title: Worked example 1
notes.problem: A scratch card costs R10. There is a 1 in 50 chance of winning R200 and a 1 in 10 chance of winning R20. Find the expected value of buying one card.
notes.answer: On average you lose R4 per card.

notes.title: Worked example 2
notes.problem: Compare the probability of serious injury for people wearing and not wearing seat belts.
steps: Not wearing a seat belt made serious injury 8 times as likely in this data.

notes.label: Relative risk
notes.text: Comparing probabilities as a ratio (40% ÷ 5% = 8) is called **relative risk**. Always also look at the actual numbers, because a large relative risk of a very rare event may still be a small risk.

notes.title: Worked example 3
notes.problem: A factory's machines produce faulty items 3% of the time. Two items are chosen at random. Find P(at least one is faulty).

questions.prompt: A forecast gives a 20% chance of rain. Which is the best interpretation?
options: It will rain for 20% of the day
On days like this, it rains about 1 in 5 times
20% of the area will get rain

questions.prompt: A game costs R5. You win R30 with a probability of $\frac{1}{8}$. What is the expected value per game, in rand? (use a minus sign for a loss)
Using the seat-belt table, what percentage of all people involved in accidents were seriously injured? (two decimals)
The probability that a component fails is 0,1. Two independent components are used. What is P(at least one fails)?
Buying more lottery tickets every week is a reliable way to grow your savings.
An insurer covers 10 000 cars. Each year about 2% are written off, with an average payout of R150 000. What minimum annual premium per car is needed to cover these payouts?
questions.memo:
✓ Expected write-offs: 2% × 10 000 = 200 (1)
✓ Total payouts: 200 × R150 000 = R30 000 000 (1)
✓ Minimum premium R3 000 per car (1)

questions.prompt: In a study, 6 out of 1 000 smokers and 1 out of 1 000 non-smokers developed a disease. Calculate the relative risk and explain what it means.
questions.memo:
✓ 0,6% and 0,1% (1)
✓ Relative risk = 6 (1)
✓ Smokers were 6 times as likely to develop the disease (1)

questions.prompt: A spinner has 5 equal sections numbered 1 to 5. It costs R4 to play and you win R15 if it lands on 5. Is the game fair? Show working.
questions.memo:
✓ P(5) = $\frac{1}{5}$ (1)
✓ Expected winnings $\frac{1}{5} \times R15 = R3$ (1)
✓ R3 < R4, so not fair: the player expects to lose R1 per game (1)

questions.prompt: Why might a positive result on a test for a rare disease still be likely to be a false positive?
questions.memo:
✓ Because the disease is rare, most people tested do not have it (1)
✓ so even a small error rate produces more false positives than true positives (1)
